title: Cosmic fireball falling over ALMA
caption: A meteor falling over ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile

recognition.text: Ranked #55 on ESO’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: A spectacular streak of light slices across the sky above the ALMA antennas in this photograph, glowing emerald green, gold and faint crimson. It is a meteor, a shooting star, burning up as it enters Earth's atmosphere. Near the centre of the image, Spica, the brightest star in Virgo, and the planet Mars shine as they rise above the horizon.

The fireball is really a small grain of rock from interplanetary space. As it plunges into the air it heats up, and its outer layers vaporise, leaving a glowing trail that vanishes within seconds. The camera caught it in a moment.

Some of ALMA's 66 high-precision antennas point skyward, studying cold clouds between the stars and looking far back towards our cosmic origins. The array sits 5000 metres above sea level on the remote Chajnantor plateau in the Chilean Andes. The photo was taken during a time-lapse sequence for the ESO Ultra HD Expedition.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph from a time-lapse sequence shot with Ultra HD camera equipment; the source gives no exposure settings.
understand.eye: A meteor lasts only seconds, and the camera freezes and records its colours and the surrounding sky more vividly than the eye could.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The photographer was Christoph Malin, an ESO Photo Ambassador who specialises in time-lapse, working on the team's eighth night at Chajnantor. The expedition, which began in Santiago, also included Herbert Zodet, Yuri Beletsky and Babak Tafreshi.
alt: A bright green, gold and crimson meteor streak above ALMA antennas, with a bright star and Mars near the centre.
